faq: Can you put a hard cap on spending?
Yes, where the provider supports it. We set spending limits in the model or tool account itself, plus a second limit inside the agent, so one failure does not remove the other.
What happens when the agent hits a limit?
It stops that action, records why and alerts the person you name. It does not look for a way around the limit. You can raise a limit later by editing one setting.
Do limits make the agent useless?
Good limits should not. We set them from what the agent really needs, then test with real work. If a limit blocks normal tasks, we adjust it in the revision period.
Can you apply limits to an agent someone else built?
Often yes, if we can see its settings and get collaborator access. We review it first and tell you which limits can be added without a rebuild.

desc:
AI agent limits, spending caps and permissions decide what your agent may do, spend and send on its own. Ecom Swift LLC writes the rules with you, builds them into the agent, and tests that they hold when the agent is pushed to break them.

## Why an unattended agent needs hard limits

An agent that works without supervision will eventually meet a case nobody planned for. It may loop and call a paid tool a thousand times, send the same message to every contact, or follow an instruction hidden in a customer email. Without limits, the only protection is hoping the model behaves.

Limits move that protection out of the prompt and into the system. A prompt can be ignored or misread. A cap on daily messages, enforced in code or in the tool's own settings, cannot be talked around. That difference is why limits are the first thing worth building before an agent is left alone.

## What counts as a limit, a permission and a rule?

A limit is a ceiling on volume or cost, such as the number of emails per day or the amount the agent may spend on paid tools. A permission is a yes or no on a type of action, such as reading orders but not editing them. A rule is any written boundary, including topics the agent must not discuss.

Together they form a policy: a short document that says what the agent may do, what it must hand to a person, and what it must never do.

## How limits affect cost, safety and trust

Cost is the easiest effect to see. A spending cap on model usage and paid tools turns an open-ended bill into a known maximum. Send limits protect your sender reputation and your customers from floods of messages.

Safety comes from narrow permissions. An agent that can only read a folder cannot delete it, however it is confused. Trust follows from both: when the team knows exactly what the agent can touch, they are willing to let it handle more real work. Good limits therefore make an agent more useful, because they remove the reasons to keep it on a short leash.

## What a strong rule set includes

- Daily and hourly caps on messages, records created and tool calls.
- A spending cap on model usage and any paid service the agent calls.
- An allowed action list and a blocked action list, kept separate.
- Different limits for different task types, since drafting differs from sending.
- Topics and content the agent must refuse, such as legal advice or medical claims.
- Permission levels per user, so a junior team member cannot widen the agent's powers.
- A stop behavior: when a rule is hit, the agent pauses and alerts a named person.
- A change log showing who altered a rule and when.
- A plain-language summary your team can read in a few minutes.

## What we do

We begin with a short interview about what your agent does today and what could go wrong. From that we draft the rules and review them with you, cutting anything that would block normal work. Then we build them in, using the controls of the agent platform, the connected tools and, where needed, a small layer of code that checks each action before it runs.

The most important step is testing. We write cases that deliberately try to break each rule: a request to exceed the cap, an instruction to use a blocked tool, a message that tries to override the policy. You see the results and any gaps we closed. The Basic, Standard and Premium packages vary by the number of rules, the number of agents covered and the reporting that comes with them.

## Do and avoid

**Do:**
- Start with tight limits and loosen them as the agent proves itself.
- Enforce limits in the system, not only in the prompt.
- Decide who gets the alert when a limit is hit.
- Retest the rules whenever the agent gains a new tool.

**Avoid:**
- Relying on the instruction "never do X" without a technical block.
- Setting one global cap that is too loose for risky tasks.
- Giving the agent an admin account because it was quicker to set up.
- Leaving limits unchanged after the agent's job has grown.
- Hiding limit alerts in a channel nobody watches.

## Who this is for

This service suits a business about to let an agent send customer messages without review. It suits a team that already runs an agent and has noticed unexpected usage costs. It also suits a manager who must show colleagues or clients that the agent works inside clear boundaries, including an agent that someone else built.

## What we need from you

Share how the agent works, what tools it uses and what worries you most. Give us access to the agent platform and its connected tools as a collaborator, team member or developer user, wherever that is supported. We never ask for passwords. All rules live in your own accounts, so you keep them if we stop working together.
